title: Preference data and Bradley-Terry reward models

key_terms.Bradley-Terry model: A comparison model in which P(a preferred over b) is the logistic function of the score difference r_a - r_b.
key_terms.Pairwise likelihood: The likelihood of observed preference outcomes, whose loss log(1 + exp(-(r_a - r_b))) is computed stably with logaddexp.
key_terms.Offset nonidentifiability: The fact that adding a constant to all scores within a prompt leaves every preference probability unchanged.
key_terms.Comparison graph: The graph of which responses were compared, whose connectivity limits which score differences are identified.

outcome: Derive a pairwise reward likelihood, test its invariances and identify what comparison data cannot determine.
verification: Equal scores give preference probability 0.5 and loss log 2, shifting both rewards changes neither loss nor gradient, reversed counts fit probability 0.25, all-win data has no finite estimate, the loss stays finite at 2000, and a preference cycle has no scalar ordering.

exercises.title: Equal scores
exercises.task: Evaluate a positive comparison when both scores are zero.
exercises.hint: Use the logistic link and softplus form.
exercises.answer: Equal scores express no preference under the model; observing a chosen response still incurs positive negative log likelihood.

reasoning.approach: Call `pair_loss([0, 0])`. The score difference is 0, so the loss is `logaddexp(0, 0)`, which is log(1 + 1) = log 2.
reasoning.why: The sigmoid of 0 is 0.5, so the model assigns equal probability to either response being preferred. Observing that the first response was chosen has probability 0.5, and its negative log is log 2, about 0.693.
reasoning.pitfall: Expecting zero loss because the scores are equal is the mistake. Zero loss would require probability 1 for the observed choice; an indifferent model still pays log 2 for every labeled comparison.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `np.isclose(pair_loss([0, 0]), np.log(2))`. Compute `sigmoid(0)` and confirm 0.5.

exercises.title: Shift both rewards
exercises.expected: Loss and score gradient remain unchanged.
exercises.answer: Pairwise labels cannot determine a common reward offset, including prompt-specific offsets when comparisons stay within prompts.

reasoning.approach: Add 100 to both scores and recompute `pair_loss` and `pair_gradient`. Case A uses `[1, -1]` and `[101, 99]`.
reasoning.why: The loss depends only on the difference a - b, which is 2 in both cases. The gradient is `[g, -g]` with g = sigmoid(2) - 1, again a function of the difference only. A common offset leaves every quantity unchanged.
reasoning.pitfall: Reading a learned reward of 101 as better than a reward of 1 from another run is the mistake. Pairwise data cannot pin down the absolute level, so rewards are only comparable within the same comparison.
reasoning.verify: Case A asserts `np.isclose(pair_loss(scores), pair_loss(shifted))`, and the exercise checks assert equal gradients for `[4, 2]` and `[104, 102]`. The gradient components also sum to 0.

exercises.title: Reverse empirical counts
exercises.task: Use one win and three losses.
exercises.answer: Reversing labels changes the sign of the fitted log odds, while finite counts still imply uncertainty.

reasoning.approach: Call `mle_difference(1, 3)`. The maximum-likelihood score difference is log(wins / losses) = log(1 / 3).
reasoning.why: The sigmoid of log(1 / 3) is (1 / 3) / (1 + 1 / 3) = 0.25, which equals the observed win fraction 1 / 4. Reversing case B's 3 to 1 counts flips the sign of the log odds and gives 0.25 instead of 0.75.
reasoning.pitfall: Reporting 0.25 as the true preference rate is too strong. With four comparisons, many probabilities near 0.25 fit nearly as well; the estimate needs an interval.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `np.isclose(sigmoid(mle_difference(1, 3)), 0.25)` and `np.isclose(mle_difference(2, 2), 0)` for balanced counts.

exercises.title: All wins and no losses
exercises.task: Fit an unregularized pair with four wins and zero losses.
exercises.hint: Log odds diverge at a boundary probability.
exercises.answer: Regularization or a prior can produce a finite estimate, but it changes the model and must be stated.

reasoning.approach: Call `mle_difference(4, 0)`. The function requires both wins and losses to be positive and raises otherwise.
reasoning.why: With four wins and zero losses, the likelihood keeps increasing as the difference grows, approaching 1 without reaching it. There is no finite maximum, so any finite number returned would be arbitrary.
reasoning.pitfall: Plugging in a tiny loss count such as 0.001 to get a finite answer is the mistake if left unstated. That is a form of regularization, and it changes the model; the chosen prior must be reported.
reasoning.verify: The reference wraps `mle_difference(4, 0)` in a try block and raises `Infinite MLE represented as finite` if no error occurs.

exercises.title: Test numerical stability
exercises.task: Use scores-1000 and 1000 for the preferred/rejected pair.
exercises.answer: Stable softplus arithmetic preserves the large finite loss without underflowing a probability to zero first.

reasoning.approach: Call `pair_loss([-1000, 1000])`. The preferred response has score -1000 and the rejected one 1000, so the difference is -2000.
reasoning.why: The loss is `logaddexp(0, 2000)`, which equals 2000 to machine precision. A naive form, -log(sigmoid(-2000)), would compute a sigmoid that underflows to 0 and then return infinity.
reasoning.pitfall: Computing the probability first and taking its log is the common error. The result is `inf` or `nan`, which then corrupts any average or gradient that includes it.
reasoning.verify: The reference asserts `np.isfinite(pair_loss([-1000, 1000]))` and that the value equals exactly 2000.

exercises.title: Interpret a preference cycle
exercises.task: Observe A>B, B>C and C>A across labels.
exercises.expected: A deterministic scalar ordering cannot satisfy all three.
exercises.hint: Add the three proposed positive score differences.
exercises.answer: Their sum would need to be positive while algebraically equaling zero. Investigate stochasticity, annotator heterogeneity and multiple criteria.

reasoning.approach: Write the three preferences as scalar inequalities: a > b, b > c and c > a. Sum the implied differences.
reasoning.why: (a - b) + (b - c) + (c - a) = 0, yet each term would need to be positive, so the sum would be positive. No scalar scores satisfy all three; case B shows a = 2, b = 1, c = 0 satisfies two but not c > a.
reasoning.pitfall: Fitting a scalar reward anyway and reporting its order as the true ranking hides the cycle. The cycle may reflect label noise, different annotators or different criteria, and each calls for a different response.
reasoning.verify: Case B asserts that `(a > b) and (b > c) and not (c > a)` for the example scores. Check cycle frequency in the raw labels before fitting.
